title: Explanation Length Distributions
takeaway: A prompting bug sometimes let Claude's whole chain of thought stand in as a feature's explanation, producing explanations several hundred tokens long instead of a few dozen. This figure shows that the long tail appears in all three scored populations at similar rates — 19% for neurons, 15% for the randomized model, 13% for the A/1 features — and the appendix reports that splitting scores into long-explanation and short-explanation groups does not change them significantly. It is a caveat check the authors ran, not a result about features.
walkthrough:
Three histograms stacked in one column, sharing a single horizontal axis: the length of the natural-language explanation that Claude 2 wrote for one unit. Each row is a different population of units. Magenta on top is the learned [[feature]] set of the A/1 [[dictionary-learning-run]]. Teal in the middle is the 512 MLP neurons of the same transformer ([[neuron-notation]]). Yellow at the bottom is the features fit to the [[randomized-transformer]] baseline. The vertical axis is density, so each row sums to one and the three can be compared even though the populations differ in size.

Why length matters at all. In [[automated-interpretability]], Claude first writes an explanation of a unit from examples of where it fires, and then, in a fresh interaction with the true activations hidden, uses only that written explanation to predict activations on new text. The score is [[activation-prediction-scoring]], a [[spearman-correlation]] between predicted and true activations.

The prompt asks Claude to reason first and place the finished explanation inside `<answer>` tags. Sometimes it fails to close them. The whole chain of thought is then kept as the explanation — the [[explanation-length-caveat]] — and that reasoning names specific tokens the unit fires on. A longer explanation could therefore make the prediction step easier and inflate the score.

How to read the rows. Each has two modes. The tall left mode, roughly 50–150 tokens, is well-formed short answers. The low, broad right mode, spread from about 500 to 1300 tokens, is leaked chain of thought.

What it shows. The right mode is present in every row, so the bug is not specific to features. By the appendix's count it is most common for neurons at 19%, then the randomized model at 15%, then features at 13% — slightly more inflation, if any, for the baselines the paper is beating.

One limit worth naming. This panel plots lengths only. The score split it is cited for is asserted in the text, with no distribution and no test statistic shown here, and the surrounding paragraph describes the measure as characters while the axis reads tokens.

terms.definition: The figure's title. It plots how long Claude's written explanations were, for each of the three populations of units that the automated interpretability pipeline scored.

The horizontal axis, shared by all three rows: the number of tokens in the text taken as a unit's explanation. Short values are properly tagged answers; long values are cases where the untrimmed chain of thought was used instead.

The vertical axis of each row: the histogram is normalized so its total area is one, rather than showing raw counts. This lets the three populations be compared even though they contain different numbers of units.
The top row, in magenta. Its units are the features learned by the A/1 sparse autoencoder on the main one-layer transformer's MLP activations.
The paper's naming scheme: model "A" and dictionary learning run "1", the run whose 4,096 features are used throughout the global analyses.
The middle row, in teal. Its units are the raw MLP neurons of transformer A, scored by exactly the same pipeline so features and neurons can be compared.

The bottom row, in yellow. Its units are features learned by dictionary learning on a version of the transformer whose weight matrices have had their entries shuffled — a control for how much of the structure comes from the model rather than the data.
A direction in activation space recovered by the sparse autoencoder, treated by the paper as the interpretable unit that should replace the neuron.

The short natural-language description Claude 2 writes of what a unit fires for, given examples of its activations. It is the only channel through which information about the unit reaches the prediction step.
The delimiters the prompt asks Claude to wrap its final explanation in, so the preceding reasoning can be stripped off. When Claude omits them, nothing gets stripped.

The step-by-step reasoning Claude produces before its final answer, demonstrated in the eight worked examples included in the prompt. When it is not stripped, it becomes part of the explanation and names concrete tokens the unit fires for.
The left annotation, pointing at the tall mode near the origin. It marks the intended behaviour: a brief answer, with the reasoning cut away.

terms.term: "Sometimes explanations are longer due to a bug..."
terms.definition: The right annotation, pointing at the low second mode. It states the authors' reading: the leakage is uncommon, occurs at similar rates in all three rows, and does not appear to move scores.
The number this caveat is about: the Spearman correlation between Claude's predicted activations and the true ones, computed per unit from the explanation alone.
Correlation computed on ranks rather than raw values, used here so a prediction only has to order tokens by activation strength correctly.
The language model that writes the explanations and then predicts activations from them. It is the explainer, not the model under study.
The shape every row has here: one narrow peak of short explanations, plus a separate low, wide bump of long ones. The second mode is the bug, not a different kind of feature.

numbers.meaning: The horizontal axis ticks, in tokens. The axis is cut at 1400 because essentially no explanation runs longer than that.
Where the tall left peak sits in every row: the length of a correctly tagged explanation, after the prompt asks Claude to be succinct and to avoid listing specific tokens.
The span of the low right mode: explanations that are really untrimmed chain of thought, roughly an order of magnitude longer than intended.
How often the long-explanation bug fires for neurons — the highest of the three rows, per the appendix text.
How often it fires for the randomized transformer's features.
How often it fires for the A/1 features — the lowest rate, so if leaked reasoning inflates scores it inflates the two comparison groups slightly more than the paper's own features.
The number of rows: A/1 features, neurons, randomized-transformer features. These are the three populations compared throughout the automated interpretability section.
The number of features in the A/1 dictionary, of which 168 dead and 292 ultralow-density features are excluded from the global analyses before any scoring.
The number of MLP neurons in the one-layer transformer, the size of the population in the middle row.

Examples shown to Claude when it writes an explanation: 10 from the top activation interval, 2 from each of the other 12 intervals, 5 random, and 10 where the top-activating token appears in other contexts.
Examples Claude then predicts activations for, using only its own explanation; at nine tokens each this gives 540 predictions per unit, which the Spearman score is computed over.
The range activations are quantized to before Claude sees or predicts them, following Bills et al. so the task is a small integer prediction.
Human-written demonstration features included in both prompts, each showing chain-of-thought reasoning — the reasoning style that leaks into the long explanations plotted here.
